results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?

status_messages.message: Refining tool choice for VFB query

results.response:
The major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body are the calyx, peduncle, and lobes. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain (VFB) database, specifically from the term info for "mushroom body" (FBbt_00005801). 

The calyx is the part of the mushroom body closest to the cortex and receives sensory interneuron afferents. The peduncle is a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes. The mushroom body lobe system consists of a vertical branch and a medial branch, which have different structures at different life stages.

According to the VFB, the mushroom body is divided into these subdivisions, and each has distinct characteristics and functions. The calyx receives sensory information, while the peduncle and lobes are involved in processing and integrating this information.

For more detailed information on the subdivisions of the mushroom body, including their specific functions and connections, it would be necessary to narrow down the query to a specific neuron class or region within the mushroom body.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The LPLC2 visual neuron type is a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron with a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer. It has presynaptic sites in layer 4 of the lobula and projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. The LPLC2 neuron is cholinergic and is involved in detecting looming (expansion) stimuli, eliciting a jump escape response. There are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe, and they are found in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind.

The LPLC2 neuron has downstream connectivity with various neuron classes, including adult VPNd1 lineage neurons, lobula plate-lobula columnar neurons LPLC2, adult cholinergic neurons, adult posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum neurons 111, and lobula plate-lobula columnar neurons LPLC4. It also has upstream connectivity with adult cholinergic neurons, T5c neurons, T5b neurons, T4c neurons, and transmedullary neurons Tm5Y.

Genetic tools available for studying LPLC2 include split-GAL4 drivers such as P{R12E04-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R19G02-p65.AD} and P{R75G12-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R19G02-p65.AD}, as well as expression patterns like P{VT007194-GAL4} and P{GMR75G12-GAL4}.

Publications related to LPLC2 include those by Wu et al. (2016), Klapoetke et al. (2017), Tanaka and Clark (2022), and Davis et al. (2020), which provide more information on the anatomy, connectivity, and function of this neuron type.

This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain (VFB) database, specifically from the neuron profile summary for LPLC2, which includes metadata, query summaries, and evidence from various sources, including publications and genetic tools.

The subesophageal zone (SEZ) is a neuropil mass below the esophagus encompassing the three gnathal neuromeres and any regions of the cephalic (supraesophageal) neuromeres situated below the esophagus. VFB has 2698 neurons with some part in the SEZ, including examples such as CB0550, CB0552, DSOG2, IB097, and SMP586. The SEZ has 122 parts, including the centromedial domain of larval maxillary neuromere, dorsolateral domain of larval maxillary neuromere, and ventrolateral domain of larval maxillary neuromere. There are 2 subclasses of the SEZ: adult subesophageal zone and larval subesophageal zone.

The medulla is divided into 10 layers, with the outer (distal) medulla consisting of layers 1-6, the seventh (or serpentine) layer exhibiting a distinct architecture, and layers 8-10 making up the inner (proximal) medulla.

Some of the neurons that have presynaptic terminals in the medulla include Mi10b, PS128, Tm39, TmY-ds, and Y5. Neurons that have postsynaptic terminals in the medulla include ML-VPN2, Mt-VPN1, T4ai neuron, T4aii neuron, and T4bi neuron.

The medulla is part of the adult optic lobe and is involved in visual processing. It receives input from various neurons, including those from the lamina and the lobula complex, and sends output to other regions, such as the lobula and the lateral horn.
